title: Ad click aggregation: count per minute, keep the raw clicks
brief: Design ad click aggregation. Each click on an ad hits a click service that records it and redirects the user to the advertiser's page. Advertisers watch clicks per ad per minute on dashboards (and often the top-K most clicked ads); billing charges advertisers per click. Clicks are writes, dashboard queries are reads. Two sim limits: a block passes on every message it gets, so the sim can't show aggregators turning 20k clicks/s into one row per ad per minute. Don't draw an edge from the aggregators to the database (it would carry every click); size that flush in estimation. And the sim counts a dashboard query as one read, however many rows it scans.

requirements: About 100k ads get at least one click in any given minute (for estimating the flush)
Aggregators only bump counters in memory: set their capacity to 5,000 clicks/s per replica (a sim estimate)
aggregation lag (backlog) under 20,000 clicks, about 1 s
clicks keep being accepted while the aggregators restart, and the lag is gone within 60 s after (the twist checks it)
variants.twist: An aggregator host crashes: kill_replica on the aggregator block for 10 s, then restore_replica. Do the rest keep up, or does lag build in the log? Then a bad deploy takes them all down: kill_node on the aggregators for 10 s, then restore_node. Clicks should keep being accepted while they wait in the log, and the lag should drain. How fast, with your spare capacity? Then talk it through: the counts for the open minute were only in memory. How does the restarted aggregator rebuild them without losing or double-counting a click? Think about when it commits its log offsets.

requirements: Billing must be exact: keep every raw click, with its click id, for 30 days, so a nightly batch job can recount them and correct the streaming totals (Kafka keeps messages 7 days by default)
A consumer that writes one raw click per store call handles about 1,000 clicks/s (the Service default, a sim estimate); aggregators 5,000 clicks/s as in dashboards

Object storage (e.g. S3) is a common raw archive too, written as batched files: one PUT per click would be about 70M PUTs an hour, roughly $350/hr in PUT fees at $0.005 per 1,000. The sim can't batch, so here use a store that takes a row per click
backlog under 20,000 in every consumer group
variants.twist: One ad goes viral: 30% of all clicks. Keyed by ad_id, they all land on one partition, and a partition is read by one consumer per group: one archiver gets about 6k clicks/s against its ~1k, one aggregator 6k against its 5k. The sim spreads a stream evenly over partitions, so it won't show this: talk it through. How do you split the hot key (e.g. ad_id plus a suffix 0-9), and where do the partial counts get merged?

hints: At 20k clicks/s, what happens to a database that gets one row per click? How many rows does a dashboard actually need per ad per minute?

Put the clicks in a partitioned log keyed by ad_id; consumers count them in memory per 1-minute window and write one row per ad per minute. Billing: can a second set of consumers read the same log, and what caps how many of them can work at once?

Dashboards: log -> aggregator consumers, enough readers for 20k/s at 5k each plus headroom to catch up after a crash; the database only serves dashboard reads. Billing: add a consumer group that writes the raw clicks to a store built for many small writes. Each group reads every message, but partitions cap the readers in each group: size the partitions for the slower group.
_notes: 20k rps, 2% reads: 19.6k clicks/s, 400 dashboard reads/s. Front: LB + 25 services (rho 0.8). Naive client -> service -> SQL: errors over 90%. 25 services -> SQL, a row per click: 19.6k writes on a 5k primary, errors over 90%. A row per click in DynamoDB: no errors but $46.72/hr (write request pricing). Dashboards intended: services -> Kafka (writes only, $0.63) -> aggregators (Service, capacity 5k), no edge out; services -> SQL (reads only, rho 0.08). Partitions = aggregators: 3 fail (backlog 69k after 15 s), 4 to 8 pass ($4.06 to $4.46; 4 runs at rho 0.98), 9 is over budget ($4.56). 2 partitions with 6 aggregators: 2 read, backlog 144k. Drawing the flush as aggregators -> SQL sends every click to SQL: backlog over 200k. Twist part 1 (one aggregator down 10 s, kill_replica): 5 don't notice (4 left = 20k/s for 19.6k clicks/s); 4 pass steady at rho 0.98 but fall 46k behind and, with 400/s spare, still hold 22k 60 s later (backlog check fails): that's N+1. Without a log, one aggregator down doesn't hurt 5 either, so part 2 is what shows the log's value. Real Kafka also pauses consumption while it moves the dead consumer's partitions to the survivors (a rebalance; how long depends on the protocol), not modeled. Twist part 2 (aggregators killed 10 s): errors ~0, backlog 196k; 5 aggregators drain it within 40 s, 4 still hold 172k after 60 s (400/s spare). Clicks straight into the aggregators (no log) pass steady ($3.53) but fail ~98% while they're down. Raw clicks straight into a 3-replica wide-column store also pass ($3.73) because query-time scans aren't modeled: ask how dashboards stay fast (pre-aggregation, or an OLAP store that rolls up on ingest). Billing: the dashboards design plus an archiver consumer group (Service, 1k/s) -> wide-column (3 replicas, rho 0.65). Partitions = archivers: 6 fail (backlog 204k), 18 fail (24k after 15 s), 19 fall behind 600/s (fail over 60 s), 20 to 26 pass ($7.36 to $7.96), 28 is over budget ($8.16). Archiver -> SQL: backlog over 200k. A PUT per click into S3: $352.80/hr in PUT fees alone (19.6k/s); behind an archiver it's over $400/hr, as redeliveries add PUTs once the sim's S3 capacity (11k/s, its GET figure) overflows. Real S3 allows about 3,500 PUTs/s per prefix, so a PUT per click would be throttled (503 Slow Down) much sooner. The sim can't tell that the billing archive is missing: the dashboards design passes billing's checks ($4.16). A dual write (services -> Kafka and services -> wide-column) passes too ($5.36), but the two writes can disagree when one fails; the raw store should be fed from the log. Grade beyond the sim: (1) API: a click endpoint (e.g. GET /click?ad_id=...&click_id=... that appends to the log and answers 302 to the landing page, never waiting on aggregation); dashboard query GET /ads/{ad_id}/clicks?from=&to= returning per-minute counts; top-K GET /ads/top?window=1m&k=100. (2) Data model: raw click event {click_id (unique, set before the first send so a retry carries the same id), ad_id, event timestamp, user or device id, IP, plus whatever billing filters on}; aggregate table keyed by (ad_id, minute) -> count, written as an upsert so a rewrite is idempotent; optionally a top-K table per window. Raw events stay in the log and in the archive for audits and recounts. (3) Trade-offs: exact vs approximate (a Count-Min Sketch, plus a small heap for top-K, estimates per-ad counts in fixed memory; it can overcount, never undercounts; billing uses exact counts); at-least-once delivery plus dedup by click_id and idempotent writes vs exactly-once processing (e.g. Flink checkpoints or Kafka transactions keep offsets and state together; end to end it still needs an idempotent or transactional sink); commit offsets only after a window is flushed, or store them in the same transaction as the counts, so a crash replays from the last flush; event time vs processing time, with a watermark and allowed lateness, and clicks later than that either update the closed window or wait for the nightly recount; reconciliation: a batch job over the raw events recomputes the counts and corrects the streaming totals before invoicing; hot ad: split the key (ad_id + suffix), aggregate the parts, then merge (per-partition top-K lists merge exactly only when each ad lives in one partition). Checked in frontend/src/lessons/content.test.ts.
